summary: This informational report records the conclusions of an IAB workshop on character sets held in early 1996. It explains why Internet protocols that carry text need character set handling, recommends tagging text using MIME, recommends a default character set, and makes recommendations to the IAB, IANA and the IESG.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2130 reports on an IAB workshop about character sets in Internet protocols. It separates the steps used to represent and transmit text, and recommends labeling those choices so receivers do not have to guess.

subtitle: An IAB workshop report on labeling text so Internet protocols can interpret it consistently.

tldr.problem: Protocols used the term character set in different ways and developed separate methods for handling text encodings.
tldr.mechanism: The report separates text transmission into a coded character set, character encoding scheme, and transfer encoding syntax, and recommends explicit labels and defaults.
tldr.outcome: It records Informational recommendations, not a standard, and has been updated by RFC 6055.

today: RFC 2130 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 6055. It records the recommendations of the IAB Character Set Workshop rather than specifying a standard.

sections.title: The Character Set Problem
sections.content:
RFC 2130 records an Internet Architecture Board (IAB)-sponsored workshop held from 29 February to 1 March 1996. The workshop aimed to guide the IAB and the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) on character sets and to develop a common framework for interoperability.

The phrase character set had different meanings in different contexts. Mail, directory, and Web protocols also developed different ways to handle the growing number of text encodings. The workshop wanted a common framework without breaking existing protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet protocols handled text in different ways, and the term character set was unclear. The workshop proposed a shared way to describe text so systems could interpret it more consistently.

sections.title: The Text Transmission Model
sections.content:
The report describes seven layers of text handling. Four relate to how people see text: layout, culture, locale, and language. Three describe text sent over a network: the Coded Character Set (CCS), the Character Encoding Scheme (CES), and the Transfer Encoding Syntax (TES).

A CCS maps abstract characters to integers. A CES maps one or more coded character sets to bytes; UTF-8 is an example for ISO 10646. A TES transforms encoded text so a protocol can transmit it; Base64 is one example. The sender should specify each transmission layer explicitly, except that language information may sometimes be implicit.
sections.plainLanguage: Text sent over a network needs three kinds of information: which characters it uses, how those characters become bytes, and whether the data is transformed for transmission.

sections.title: Labels and Recommended Defaults
sections.content:
A receiver can learn encoding labels from the protocol standard, an attached header, the data itself, prior agreement, negotiation, or by guessing. The report says guessing is not reliable. It recommends using registered Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) values for character-set and language labels unless another established method already provides the information.

The report recommends ISO 10646 as the default coded character set. New text-oriented protocols should use UTF-8 as their character encoding scheme; protocols with backward-compatibility needs should retain their existing defaults. It recommends that protocols state their choices clearly and that stored text be tagged so it can be interpreted later. These defaults do not deprecate other character sets.
sections.plainLanguage: Receivers need labels that say how text was encoded. The report recommends explicit labels and suggests ISO 10646 and UTF-8 as defaults for new protocols, while allowing other choices when needed.

sections.title: Converting Between Character Sets
sections.content:
If every character in the source set is also available in the target set, the report calls the conversion exact. The characters stay the same; only their byte representations need to be remapped.

Otherwise, the converted text differs from the original. For display, a conversion may use one or more target characters that resemble the source. If the target must stay the same length, each source character maps to one target character. For fully reversible conversion, the report describes using an escape-style encoding so the original text can be recovered.
sections.plainLanguage: Conversion can preserve the text exactly when the target set contains every source character. If it does not, a conversion may replace characters with similar ones or use a reversible encoding.

sections.title: Open Issues and Recommendations
sections.content:
The workshop left several issues open, including how to represent non-ASCII characters in public identifiers, how to handle bidirectional text, and how to select national variants of shared Han characters. It recommended support for language tagging in new protocols and recommended using MIME's Content-Language header to identify the language of text.

The report recommends that new protocols use ISO 10646 as their base character set unless there is an overriding reason not to, use registered values for parameters, and tag text with its language. It says there are no security considerations associated with character sets and concludes that the framework could support interoperability while open issues remain.
sections.plainLanguage: The report recommends that new protocols label text and identify its language. It also records unresolved questions about identifiers, right-to-left text, and how shared characters should appear in different languages.
